voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: As the owner remembers it, the text said: I paid him cash, like you said. He hadn't said that.

Pearl's Bagels, in Northwest D.C. A Saturday morning in April, twenty twenty-three, at its busiest. A man with a notepad said he was there to inspect the fire-suppression system, for the company that services their equipment.
He used the owner's name, and asked to speak with him. On the phone, he told the owner, Oliver Cox, he'd update the tags and come back Monday with new parts. The system was due for service.
Then he hung up, and told the manager the owner had said to pay in cash. She hadn't heard the call. Four invoices. Nine hundred and seventy dollars, from the register.
He said he'd be back in three minutes. He never returned. The invoices were from Metro Fire Prevention, a company the shop says doesn't exist. The address had no quadrant.

Reporters found at least six similar cases up and down the East Coast. It hasn't been determined that one man did them all. Two lies, told apart. To the owner, a routine service call. To the manager, the owner's permission. Neither heard the other's.
